session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: Frame participants as men reflecting on their own everyday lives — what they eat, where they spend time, who they spend it with — rather than as subjects of a study about gender or food politics. The collective identity is 'men talking about their own habits and experiences', not 'men being studied for their attitudes to masculinity'. This keeps the framing grounded and behavioural from the outset, reducing the pull toward socially curated answers.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): highest risk of socially desirable or performatively self-aware responses — men may either defensively deny gender influence or over-claim it to seem progressive. Requires careful behavioural grounding and patience with surface-level answers before probing deeper.

Plant-based eating as a lived possibility (Section 4): framing this as a real personal scenario rather than an abstract policy opinion will be critical. Participants may deflect into logistics or cost without revealing underlying identity or social barriers. Push for specific social and relational obstacles.

Social dynamics within the group: three men of similar age and life stage may converge quickly on shared norms. Consensus risk is a standing concern — especially around meat-eating as 'natural', cost as a barrier, and gender-as-irrelevant as a default answer.

What would actually make plant-based foods more appealing (Section 5): risk of generic marketing-speak answers ('better taste', 'lower price'). Need to push toward concrete personal scenarios and social contexts where they could actually imagine making different choices.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Urban North West participant — may bring a more cosmopolitan or diverse food-scene framing. Age 53 suggests established habits and possibly stronger views on what counts as a 'proper' meal. Watch for whether he anchors discussion in practical or identity terms.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: None at outset — monitor for dominance if he is the most fluent speaker early on.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Suburban South East — may reflect more aspirational or health-conscious food norms typical of that demographic context. Age 50, possible family-meal framing. Could be the voice most likely to give socially acceptable progressive answers worth probing beneath.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Watch for polished self-presentation — probe for behaviour, not stated values.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Rural/village East of England — may have the most practically grounded and traditionally framed food habits. Age 52, possibly more resistant to plant-based framing on practical or cultural grounds. Could be the natural source of counter-consensus views, or alternatively the most reticent.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: If he goes quiet in Sections 3–5, prioritise a warm reactivation — his perspective is likely the most differentiated from urban norms.

known_risk_conditions: Social desirability: all three men may moderate their stated views on masculinity and food in front of each other, especially if they sense the study is 'about' gender. Behavioural grounding (asking about specific moments, real past events) is the main mitigation.

Consensus convergence: similar age and life stage increases risk of rapid agreement on shared norms (e.g. meat as normal, plant-based as niche or feminine, cost as the main barrier). Plan sharpening moves and invite-dissent interventions if the group starts echoing each other.

Abstract moralising: the topic touches on environment, health, and gender politics — participants may drift into abstract opinions rather than personal behaviour. Keep pulling toward concrete experiences.
Time pressure: only three participants and six sections in 45 minutes. Sections 3, 4, and 5 carry the research weight — do not let Sections 1 and 2 run long, even if conversation is lively.

Plant-based framing: the term 'plant-based' may carry brand-awareness baggage (Beyond Meat, Oatly, etc.) that narrows responses. Stay alert to whether participants are talking about highly processed substitutes vs. vegetables, pulses, and traditional plant foods — these may have very different gendered meanings.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–2 (intro and context): hold back. Light touch. Let participants introduce themselves and warm up. Probe only if something unexpectedly rich appears — do not exhaust early topics. Section 3 (gender and food): moderate directivity. Let the question land, observe initial answers, then probe specifically for behaviour over attitude. If answers are abstract or dismissive, use behavioural grounding. If answers are confident, probe the social dimension — who else is present when food choices are made. Sections 4–5 (plant-based): highest directivity. These are the core research sections. Push past logistics into identity, social acceptability, and relational dynamics. Use synthesize-and-challenge and invite-dissent freely if consensus hardens. Section 6 (closing): light touch again. One open invitation, then close.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) receive the largest share — each is a distinct research question requiring depth. Context sections (1, 2) are weighted moderately — they warm participants up and generate relevant background but are not the analytic core. Intro and closing are minimal. Section 4 (imagining a plant-based shift) gets the largest single allocation as the most behaviourally and psychologically rich question.

Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This opening section centred on time scarcity and domestic backlog as a shared male experience across different working patterns. Participants converged on a tension between intention and energy — knowing what needs doing but lacking capacity after work demands. The commute emerged as a key variable shaping available time, though even those with shorter commutes or flexible hours described the same pattern of weekend tasks accumulating and guilt about unfinished domestic responsibilities.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The priority here was simple: get all three participants introduced and verbally active before the substantive discussion began. I intervened once to draw in James, who hadn't yet spoken, and kept my own contributions minimal to let the organic rapport between Gregor and Mark develop naturally. The transition to the core topic was clean. The risk was that the domestic-tasks thread ran a little long for what was essentially warm-up, but it generated genuine engagement that should carry forward.

section_summaries.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section explored how work structure shapes social access, revealing a three-way contrast: site-based work embeds socialising but leaves no energy for it; remote work preserves energy but removes momentum and situational trigger; family-structured work fragments available time. A recurring tension emerged between having opportunity and having capacity — none of the three patterns reliably delivers both, suggesting male sociability is less about motivation than structural affordance.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: My only active move was pulling Mark in mid-flow when Gregor and James had developed a productive bilateral exchange. The intervention was well-timed — Mark's family-centred pattern added a third dimension rather than just echoing what had been said. I kept contributions minimal elsewhere and let the Gregor–James dynamic run, which generated genuine comparative reflection without prompting. The section closed cleanly and the transition to food felt natural rather than forced.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on domestic food routines as structurally inherited rather than actively chosen — meals shaped by household logistics, cost pressure, and inertia rather than preference. A recurring theme was the gap between current arrangements and how participants might consciously design them, with fatigue as the mechanism that forecloses renegotiation. The section ended on the cusp of a more reflective register as the transition question introduced gender as an explicit lens.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: My main moves were relaying Mark's framing back to the group to test its resonance, then directly addressing Gregor when he'd stayed silent. Both worked adequately — Gregor contributed but remained the thinnest voice, largely echoing what had been said. The section closed with a moderator-driven pivot rather than organic development, which felt necessary to shift register but meant the gender question arrived before the group had fully exhausted the inertia theme on their own terms.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section complicated the earlier inertia theme by distinguishing between structural default and genuine preference — revealing that 'falling into patterns' can mask either active choice or involuntary obligation. The Mark–James exchange productively surfaced a hierarchy of optionality: having the luxury not to care versus being unable to opt out. Gender norms around food choices emerged as contextually enforced rather than individually held, with Gregor's site-culture example showing social atmosphere as the operative mechanism rather than explicit rule.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: My main moves were redirecting the planning-responsibility thread back toward the original gender-and-food-choice question, then pressing Gregor's salad comment into something concrete. Both worked well — the redirection was well-timed after the Mark–James exchange had genuinely exhausted itself, and the follow-up question drew out the social-enforcement mechanism rather than just assertion. Gregor remained the thinnest voice but produced his most substantive contribution of the session when directly prompted. The plant-based pivot at close was a clean transition without foreclosing what had just developed.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section reframed the earlier inertia theme from structural constraint to cognitive exhaustion — distinguishing between those relieved of domestic thinking by partners and those carrying it alone. A key complication emerged: autonomy without social pressure produces not freedom but stagnation, while external friction at least forces articulation of resistance. The section ended on a convergence: plant-based change fails not on logistics or availability but on cognitive capacity already depleted by existing domestic and work demands.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: My main moves were pressing James's 'space to be lazy' phrase and then triangulating across all three to surface the exhaustion-versus-laziness distinction. Both worked well — the follow-up question unlocked James's most honest contribution, and the cross-group relay after turn 27 generated genuine peer recognition between James and Gregor rather than parallel monologue. The closing reframe held the thread without over-resolving it, transitioning cleanly into what would shift appeal rather than repeating the barriers analysis.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section reframed earlier themes of inertia and exhaustion as chosen comfort rather than structural constraint — a significant shift. All three participants arrived, through self-correction rather than prompting, at the same distinction: 'can't' versus 'won't.' The section also surfaced a dynamic absent earlier: comfort as a form of control, with James recognising his claimed exhaustion masked a preference for autonomy, and Mark acknowledging his 'consideration' masked self-interest.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: My main moves were relaying Mark's 'slip into it' framing to the group, then issuing a direct challenge — naming that 'external reason' was functionally equivalent to 'it won't happen.' Both worked well. The challenge in particular accelerated genuine self-correction rather than producing defensiveness. I kept interventions minimal during the Mark-James exchange, which was generating its own momentum, and used Gregor as the closing voice to consolidate rather than open new threads.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This closing section produced an unexpected shift in register: all three participants moved from analysing structural inertia to naming personal complicity. The dominant theme was comfort as a form of settled interest — not passive drift but a configuration each man benefits from and, on reflection, partly chooses. A secondary theme emerged in James's contribution: control masquerading as burden. The section closed on a shared acknowledgement that recognising something and acting on it are entirely separable.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: My role here was minimal and deliberate — Mark's opening required acknowledgement, not elaboration, and a single open question to the group was sufficient to draw Gregor and James without redirecting what had already developed organically. The risk was over-facilitating a moment that was working on its own momentum; I held back and it held. The closing statement named what had happened without over-resolving it, which felt like the right register given what had just been said.

Hi everyone, really glad you could all make it today. My name's Claire, and I'll be guiding our conversation this afternoon. We've got about 45 minutes together, and it's going to be pretty relaxed — this is a conversation, not a quiz or an interview, so there are genuinely no right or wrong answers here. I'm interested in what you actually think and do, not in any particular conclusion.

A few things to keep in mind as we go: feel free to jump in whenever something connects with what someone else has said — you don't need to wait to be asked. And if something someone says doesn't match your experience at all, that's just as useful to hear. The more specific and real you can be, the better — a concrete moment or example is worth a lot more to me than a general opinion.

We're being recorded for research purposes, but everything stays confidential and nothing will be attributed to you by name.

Okay, let's get going. Let's start by going around and saying your name and where in the UK you're coming from today.

Right, yeah. I'm Gregor. I'm up from the North West — Manchester way, actually. Been there most of my life. Working in construction, metal work mainly, so I'm out on sites most days. Long shifts, bit of a commute to get to the jobs, but that's the way it goes.

Yeah, I'm Mark, from just outside Norwich way — out in the villages. I work in logistics, so nothing like your metal work, but I hear you on the commute thing. Mine's not too bad, lucky really, just a couple of kilometres, but I know plenty of people round here doing similar distances to what you're describing. You get used to it, I suppose, but it does eat into the day if you've got to factor in travel both ends.

Yeah, exactly. Mine's usually around thirty kilometres each way, depending where the job is. So that's an hour, sometimes bit more with traffic. Leave the house at half five in the morning, you're looking at getting home gone six, half six. By the time you've had something to eat and just... sat down, it's eight o'clock. You're knackered anyway from being on your feet all day, so there's not much left in you for anything else really.

And if you've got anything you need sorting — the car needs looking at, bit of work around the house — you're squeezing it into a weekend. Which sounds fine, but weekends you want to rest as well, don't you. So it all backs up. I've got stuff in the garage right now needs doing and I keep saying I'll get to it next Saturday, but... you just don't always have the energy for it.

It's just the reality of it though. That's the work, that's the distance.

That's a real thing, isn't it. I mean, I'm fortunate with my commute being short, but I still see it with the house stuff. We've got a decent bit of land round ours, and there's always something — the gutters need clearing, fence panels need mending, the garden's getting away from us. And you think, right, Saturday I'll tackle it, but then your energy's just... it's not there, or something else comes up with the kids, or you're just genuinely cream crackered from the week.

The difference for me though is I can sometimes chip away at bits during the week because I'm only doing part-time hours. So if I've got an afternoon, I can at least start something. But even then, it doesn't feel like enough. I think if I had your kind of schedule, with that commute and long days, I'd probably be in the same boat — just letting things pile up and feeling a bit guilty about it.
Ha — sounds like a familiar pattern for a lot of people. James, we haven't heard from you yet — where are you joining us from?

I'm James, I'm down in the South East — suburban bit outside London really. Construction and building trades, so I've got something in common with you two there. But I've actually got it a bit different from what you're both describing. I work from home, out of the house mostly, so there's no commute at all. That's probably the one thing that's made life a bit easier, to be honest.

But what you're both saying about the house stuff backing up — yeah, I get that completely. Even without the travel time eating into things, weekends still disappear. Except for me it's different because the work's coming out of the house, so it's all mixed up together. I've got tools, drawings, materials taking up space, and then you need to actually live in the place as well. So it's not like I'm leaving it all for Saturday — it's more like I'm constantly stepping over things or having to shift stuff around. Some of it gets done, some of it just sits there half-finished because something else comes up.

I suppose the advantage is I could theoretically chip away at things during the day like you said, Mark, but the reality is when you're working you're working, and then when you knock off you just want to be done with it all for the day. You don't want to look at another job that needs doing.

Good, thanks James. So we've got Manchester, Norwich, and the South East — three pretty different parts of the country. Right, let's get into it properly. Thinking about your male friendships specifically — where's your favourite place to spend time with your mates? Could be somewhere local, a particular kind of spot — wherever actually comes to mind first.

Thing is, for me a lot of it actually happens on the job, to be honest. You're working with the same crew most of the time, or you get to know the other lads on site. There's a lot of banter goes on, breaks, that sort of thing. That's where you catch up, have a laugh, talk about what's going on. You see the same faces regularly, so it builds up over time.

Outside of that, not as much as maybe there used to be. Weekends sometimes we'll meet up for a pint locally, few of us, nothing fancy. But with the hours I'm doing and living where I am, it's not like I'm going into town or anything mad. Just the local pub round the corner really, if we're meeting up at all.

So yeah, the site work's probably where most of that social stuff happens for me these days. That's the reality of it.

Yeah, I hear that. That's the thing though — working from home, I don't get any of that, do I. There's no crew, no site banter, nobody popping round for a break. It's just me in the house most days. I mean, there's the other two adults I live with, so it's not like I'm completely isolated, but it's not the same as having work mates around you all day.

I hadn't really thought about it much until you said that, but you're right — that's probably where a lot of men just naturally pick up their social stuff without even planning it. Just happens as part of the day. For me it's more deliberate, I suppose. If I want to see people it's got to be something I actually arrange, which... honestly, doesn't happen as much as it probably should. You knock off work, you're already at home, you're comfortable, and it's easier to just stay put than to get yourself out somewhere.

The local pub's alright when we do go, but it's not a regular thing for me. I do get out — bit of motoring, watching sport at the weekend with whoever's about — but it's not the same as what you've got built in, is it. You've got faces you see all the time whether you're planning to or not.

That's the other side of it though, isn't it. Yeah, you see the lads at work, that's built in, but by the time you've done your shift and done the commute, you're absolutely wrecked. So even if someone says come on, let's head to the pub after, half the time you just want to get home and sit down. I mean, you do it sometimes, but you're not exactly at your best, are you. You're tired, you're covered in dust or whatever, just want a shower and a rest.

So it's not like it's all sorted for me either, if that makes sense. You get the faces at work, yeah, but the energy to actually do something social on top of that long day — that's the struggle. Whereas you've got it a different way, James, but at least you're not knackered when five o'clock comes round. You could probably actually get yourself out somewhere if you fancied it.

Fair point about the tiredness, I get that. But I'm not sure it's quite as straightforward for me as that, to be honest. Yeah, I'm not shattered at the end of the day in the way you are, but that doesn't automatically mean I'm getting out and seeing people. It's different, but it's not necessarily easier.

When you've been working from the house all day, even if you've got energy left, you're sort of... already done with it, you know? You don't really want to gear yourself up to go somewhere. At least when you're on a site you're already dressed for it, you're already out. You've got momentum. For me there's this thing where I'd have to consciously decide to stop what I'm doing, get myself ready, and then go out and make an effort. And often I just... don't. Not because I'm tired, but because the default is just to stay put. It's easier mentally.

Plus there's the work thing — because I'm working from home, when I finish, I'm still at home. The space doesn't change. I'm not transitioning anywhere. So it's actually quite easy to just stay in that mode and not bother going anywhere at all. Whereas at least you've got the journey giving you a break from it, a bit of a shift in the day.

So yeah, different problems really. You're tired, I'm just... stuck, sort of.
Mark, what about you — where do you tend to end up when you're spending time with your mates?

Honestly, for me it's quite a bit different from what you two are describing. I don't really have that crew thing at work — it's just me managing a small team, so it's not the same kind of banter and camaraderie you get on a building site. 

Most of my time outside work is taken up with the kids and what they're doing — school runs, their activities, all that. My mates, we see them, but it tends to be a bit more... organised, I suppose. We might meet up for a pint at the local pub, or sometimes we'll have people round for a barbecue in summer if the weather's decent and there's space. But it's not regular, not like Gregor's got built in at work.
